bib.title: Generalized Linear Models and Regression Trees (Chapter 8 of Computer Age Statistical Inference)

question: How do generalized linear models (logistic, Poisson, general exponential family) and regression trees bring indirect evidence from covariates to bear on a case, and what inference do they support?
contributions: Logistic regression as binomial exponential-family GLM with least-total-deviance fitting (8.1)
GLM theory: sufficient statistic z=X'y, MLE equation, concavity, Hoeffding's lemma (8.2)
Poisson regression for density estimation from truncated counts (8.3)
Regression trees by recursive partitioning, three uses of a regression rule (8.4)

limits: Chapter is expository: fits are shown for illustration, with no held-out accuracy for the spam logistic fit.
Tree error rates are apparent (training) rates; authors note bagging improves them (Ch 17, 20).
Authors concede trees are unstable, easy to overinterpret, and their discontinuous surface disqualifies them for estimation.
The 57-variable MLE is unstable; shrinkage deferred to Ch 16.
Text extraction lost minus signs and Greek glyphs; equations must be checked against the PDF.
practices: Prefer the regression-line value over the single direct observation when covariate structure exists (Sec 8 intro).
Use the logit link because it keeps probabilities in [0,1] and gives a two-number sufficient statistic (S0,S1) (Sec 8.1).
Fit GLMs by least total deviance; solve X'(y - mu(alpha)) = 0 numerically since likelihood is concave (Sec 8.2).
Check Poisson GLM fit with sum of squared deviance residuals, expected about the number of bins if the model is right (Sec 8.3).
Use Poisson regression to reduce density estimation to regression (Sec 8.3).
Pick tree splits by minimising pooled child sum of squares and stop using cross-validated prediction error (Sec 8.4).
Treat trees as prediction components (use 1), not for estimation (Sec 8.4).

terms.definition: theta = log{pi/(1-pi)}, increasing from -inf to inf as pi goes from 0 to 1
D(f1,f2) = 2 * integral f1(y) log(f1(y)/f2(y)) dy; twice the Kullback-Leibler distance; zero only if f1=f2, not symmetric
exponential family y_i ~ f_{theta_i} with natural parameters theta = X alpha, N parameters reduced to p
in expectation parametrisation the MLE of mu is y and f_mu(y) = f_y(y) exp(-D(y,mu)/2)
regression surface formed by recursive partitioning of predictor space; each terminal node predicts the node mean
bioassay with Pr{X<=x} = Phi(a0 + a1 x); logistic regression replaces Phi with the logistic cdf
